Brazilian officials first raised concerns with Apple about gambling apps accessible to minors nearly three months ago, and Apple has now been given a five-business-day deadline to provide further details on its App Store safeguards. Here are the details of the case.

Apple Pressed on Regulation and Age Verification

Last April, Brazilian officials issued notices to Apple and Google separately over alleged lack of age restrictions on gambling apps in the two companies' app stores.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) each wrote to the two companies, asking about the existence of "countless apps" offering or facilitating minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed a new law called the "ECA Digital Law," which requires app stores to restrict minors' access to gambling content. Apple subsequently introduced age verification measures for 18-rated apps in the country.

However, officials said their preliminary investigation found that many gambling apps appeared to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, raising questions about the effectiveness of the safeguards in place.

Though Apple's full response was not made entirely public, the agencies have now said Apple has addressed most of their initial questions. They are still requesting additional information.

Quoted from the Brazilian Ministry of Justice and Public Security (via Canaltech):

The clarifications sought include: how regulatory authorisation is verified for apps offered in Brazil; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation apps from those involving real-money gambling, including cases where functionality is hidden or altered after approval; and the mechanisms in place to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Authorities also requested information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, average takedown time after detection, and the published timeline for implementing corrective measures—including software updates designed to prevent users under 18 from downloading apps classified as unsuitable for that age group.

The two secretariats noted that Google's response fell short of expectations and asked for more detailed information on: how the company verifies authorised operators, how it monitors apps whose licences have been revoked or have expired, how it measures enforcement effectiveness, and how it prevents minors from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Finally, the two secretariats requested that Apple's and Google's responses be made public, while allowing confidential information to be submitted separately under restricted access.
